tier_reason: First-party hyperfine numbers with public harness code (scripts/bench_all_parsers.sh) and a named CPU (Ryzen 3900X), but no compiler versions for either side, libevtx is cloned at an unpinned HEAD and built with no explicit CFLAGS, and the current README's libevtx figure is carried over from a January 2026 run while the evtx columns were re-measured in June 2026, so the headline 34x is a cross-run ratio; not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Current README (June 2026, evtx 0.12.2 PGO build, bench commit 99a6def), 30 MB security_big_sample.evtx to XML: evtx 71.6 ms on 1 thread, 20.7 ms on 8 threads, 22.1 ms on 24 threads vs libevtx (C) 2.439 s, about 34x on one thread and 118x on 8 threads (derived from page data), but the libevtx figure is carried over unchanged from the January 2026 run, so these ratios compare two runs. Same-run numbers are in the January 2026 README (commit b2f4cba, bench commit e01782a, Linux 6.17.9): evtx 275.9 ms (1 thread), 96.9 ms (8 threads), 79.5 ms (24 threads) vs libevtx 2.439 s, about 8.8x single-threaded and 31x at 24 threads (derived from page data). README text: 'faster than any other implementation by order(s) of magnitude'.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: evtx: Cargo release profile opt-level 3, codegen-units 1, lto thin; README numbers come from build_pgo.sh (RUSTFLAGS -Cprofile-generate then -Cprofile-use, features fast-alloc (tikv-jemallocator) and wevt_templates); rustc version not stated. The committed bench script itself builds a plain 'cargo build --release --bin evtx_dump' without fast-alloc or PGO (README says PGO is worth 2-5%). libevtx: scripts/bench_all_parsers.sh clones libyal/libevtx at HEAD (unpinned), runs synclibs.sh/autogen.sh, './configure --enable-static --disable-shared --enable-static-executables' and make with no CFLAGS (autoconf default, normally -g -O2); C compiler and version not stated.
corrections.hardware: 12-core AMD Ryzen 3900X, Arch Linux; evtx columns measured June 2026 on Linux 7.0.11-arch1-1 (bench commit 99a6def), libevtx figure from the January 2026 run on Linux 6.17.9-arch1-1 (bench commit e01782a); hyperfine, 2 warmups and 5 runs by script default.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 966 stars, 86 forks; evtx crate 310,212 downloads on crates.io (latest 0.12.3, 2026-09-22); PyPI wheel via pyevtx-rs
corrections.caveats: Category fit is weak: the input is a binary log format (binary XML templates) and the output is XML text. The headline 34x/118x ratios in the current README are cross-run: the evtx columns were re-measured in June 2026 after the compiled-template rewrite while the libevtx 2.439 s figure was carried over from January 2026 (different kernel); the only same-run comparison is January 2026 (8.8x single-threaded, 31x at 24 threads). Optimisation levels are not matched: evtx uses opt-level 3, thin LTO, codegen-units 1, PGO and jemalloc, libevtx is a stock autoconf build (likely -g -O2, no LTO or PGO) at an unpinned HEAD. The committed bench script does not reproduce the PGO/jemalloc binary the README measured. No check that evtxexport -f xml and evtx_dump emit equivalent XML. The multi-thread columns compare a parallel program against single-threaded evtxexport. First-party, one machine, one input file, compiler versions absent. The speed-up is a design win (per-template compiled output, SIMD UTF-16 escaping, arena allocation), not a language-level one.
corrections.why_faster: docs/compiled-templates.html: each of the log's 32 distinct templates is compiled once into pre-rendered output text plus fill-in instructions, so per record evtx only reads the value table and copies text (no per-record tree build or re-walk, about 3x over 0.12.1); plus utf16-simd escaping, bumpalo arenas, jemalloc (fast-alloc), PGO and, for the multi-thread columns, rayon parallel chunk parsing. libevtx re-parses binary XML per record through libyal's layered C libraries. Design and algorithm, not language.

notes: Downgrade A to C: no compiler versions, unpinned libevtx built at autoconf default flags, and the current README's 34x pairs a June 2026 evtx run with a January 2026 libevtx run; use the January same-run 8.8x (1 thread) as the solid figure. Shortcomings: cross-run headline ratio, unmatched opt levels (PGO+LTO+jemalloc vs default -O2), no output-equivalence check, parallel vs single-threaded columns, weak string-and-text fit.

tier_reason: Public harness benches/compare (vendor/build.sh builds GMime, VMime, libEtPan! and Dovecot lib-mail from SHA-256-pinned sources at -O3; build.rs compiles the shims at opt_level 3; criterion bench benches/compare.rs) with compiler versions (rustc 1.98.1, Apple clang 21.0.0), flags and CPU (Apple M4) stated in README and results/summary.md, plus a published equivalence check (results/check.md); every README number matches summary.md.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Rust side: mail-parser 1.0.0 from the repository (the unreleased rewrite; crates.io latest is 0.11.9, which the harness also measures but the published tables leave out), feature full_encoding, rustc 1.98.1, release profile (opt-level 3, debug line-tables only; no LTO or PGO set), criterion 0.8.2. C/C++ side (benches/compare/README.md, vendor/build.sh OPT=-O3): Apple clang 21.0.0 (clang-2100.3.34.2); GMime 3.2.15 configure CFLAGS=-O3 --disable-crypto; VMime master 5b01911 CMake Release CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE='-O3 -DNDEBUG'; libEtPan! 1.10.1, 22 parser sources compiled at -O3; Dovecot 2.4.5 lib-mail/lib-charset/lib configure CFLAGS=-O3; shims compiled by build.rs at opt_level 3 (-std=gnu11, -std=c++17). GLib (Homebrew 2.90.0) and the macOS system iconv used for charset conversion are prebuilt system libraries, not built by the harness.
corrections.hardware: Apple M4 Mac mini (4 performance and 6 efficiency cores, 16 GB), macOS 26.6.2, measured 2026-09-28; median over three runs of criterion's median (30 samples, 3 s measurement, 0.5 s warm-up), runs gated on a machine-wide idle lock.
corrections.claimed_speedup: README, geometric mean over the corpora shown in the README tables (7 corpora for full, 6 for headers and structure), with range: full workload 31x GMime (13 to 177), 20x VMime (7.8 to 80), 15x libEtPan! (5.7 to 69), 9.3x Dovecot (4.4 to 24), 3.0x mailparse; headers 14x GMime, 33x VMime, 19x libEtPan!, 5.2x Dovecot; structure 14x GMime, 31x VMime, 17x libEtPan!, 3.9x Dovecot. Example, full workload, Enron 3,000 messages: mail-parser 2,420 MiB/s vs GMime 65, VMime 70, libEtPan! 96, Dovecot 366 MiB/s (results/summary.md: 37.10x, 34.77x, 25.23x, 6.60x).
corrections.stars_or_usage: 462 stars, 64 forks; mail-parser crate 4,234,073 downloads on crates.io (latest release 0.11.9); parser inside Stalwart Mail Server
corrections.caveats: The measured mail-parser is 1.0.0 from the repository, an unreleased rewrite; the latest crates.io release (0.11.9) decodes every body during parse and is not in the published tables. First-party harness, but results/check.md shows equal message, part and leaf counts on Enron and the generated corpora and decoded bytes within 2% on the test suites (Dovecot -6%); mailparse and Dovecot dashes-crlf cells do work that is not comparable (excluded from README tables); GMime finds no From mailbox in 327 Enron messages. Wins include lazy decoding: headers and structure never decode bodies, so large-attachment corpora reach 80,868 MiB/s. C/C++ libraries are driven through project-written shims, built without crypto, SSL and other optional features; charset conversion goes through macOS's system iconv and the C shims validate UTF-8 with GLib's g_utf8_validate_len, while mail-parser uses its own decoders and simdutf8, so part of the full-workload gap is library choice outside the parser. GMime, VMime and libEtPan! copy the input or bodies as their users would. One machine (Apple M4, NEON path); the AVX2/SSE2 x86-64 path is not measured. The nearest competitor is the Rust mailparse crate, 2.8x to 3.2x behind. Wins come from SIMD kernels, perfect hashing, lazy and zero-copy design, not from the language alone.

notes: Confirm A; numbers match README and results/summary.md, harness flags and compiler versions are stated, equivalence check exists. Correct the measured version (repository 1.0.0, unreleased, not 0.11.9). Shortcomings: first-party shims, lazy decoding inflates headers/structure ratios, system iconv/GLib on the C side, Apple M4 only.

tier_reason: First-party benchmark with public harness code (crates/ferrocat-bench/src/compare/operations.rs) and checked-in JSON reports naming rustc and the CPU (Apple M1 Ultra), but msgmerge's build flags and compiler are not stated, so not A; no independent measurement, so not B.

Per-operation times in gettext-workflows-ecosystem-v1-c3caa27.json (derived from page data): ferrocat merge 6.94 ms vs msgmerge 398.6 ms raw or 391.6 ms after subtracting a 7.0 ms empty-run baseline (about 56x); ferrocat update_catalog_file 11.85 ms vs msgmerge 392.9 ms adjusted (about 33x). The earlier a84e6fb report gives 7.9 ms vs 418.1 ms (merge, about 53x) and 16.7 ms vs 415.6 ms (update, about 25x).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Ferrocat: rustc 1.95.0-nightly (842bd5be2 2026-01-29), workspace release profile lto = fat, codegen-units = 1 (default opt-level 3), ferrocat 2.2.0 at commit c3caa27. msgmerge: GNU gettext-tools 1.0 binary from the host, invoked as 'msgmerge --no-wrap --quiet --no-fuzzy-matching existing.po template.pot' with stdout captured; its compiler and build flags are not stated.
corrections.hardware: Apple M1 Ultra, 64 GB RAM, macOS arm64 (report environment block); 2 warmup and 5 measured samples per scenario.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 0 stars, 0 forks (525 commits); ferrocat crate 7,706 downloads on crates.io (latest 3.4.2, 2026-08-06)
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark, one machine; msgmerge build flags unknown, so optimisation levels cannot be compared. The harness is fairer than it first looks: msgmerge runs with --no-fuzzy-matching (exact identity, like ferrocat), every implementation's output has the same semantic digest per fixture, and the published msgmerge MiB/s subtracts a header-only empty-run baseline (about 7 ms) to remove process start-up. Remaining asymmetries: ferrocat reads the template and existing catalog from in-memory strings inside the timed loop while msgmerge reads two files and writes to a pipe from a fresh process; MiB/s counts output bytes, and ferrocat's merge output is about 7% larger per operation than msgmerge's (2,115,311 vs 1,971,324 bytes), so the merge MiB/s ratio (61x) overstates the time ratio (56x); the README full-update cell (150 MiB/s) comes from a different report than the msgmerge cell. Numbers were measured on ferrocat 2.2.0; the current release is 3.4.2. Zero stars, so the project is unproven in the field. The speed-up is design (byte-oriented scanning, move-not-clone merge paths) against a general GNU tool, not a language-level effect.

Shortcomings: first-party, msgmerge flags unknown, in-memory vs file I/O asymmetry, output-byte MiB/s metric, 0 stars.
